 What The Surviving Cast Of Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman Looks Like Today
 By   Kyan Patten 
 Nov. 3, 2026 6:15 pm EST 
 Michelle Neese/Getty Images 
 Add The List on Google: 
 Preferred Source 
 Google Discover 
 Premiering on CBS in 1993, "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" was a woman-led western drama that many executives deemed unlikely to succeed. However, Jane Seymour — who played the lead — saw potential in the post-Civil War piece when others, including CBS, didn't. With its premise of a former Boston physician becoming the dedicated doctor for a small town in Colorado Springs, "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" tackled systemic issues that existed in both past and present times. Through 6 seasons and 150 episodes, the series thrived against early adversity. Its success is partly due to  the illustrious cast of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," some of whom are no longer with us today, like Georgann Johnson, Larry Sellers, and Orson Bean.
 Despite the series' tragic losses, the legacy of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" lives on through its surviving actors. Over the years, they've garnered enough success to overshadow their stint on the CBS original through entrepreneurship, academia, and other Hollywood accolades. To discover the whereabouts of our favorite Colorado Springs residents, here is what the surviving cast of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" has been up to over the years!
 Jane Seymour remained a prominent actor
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Jason Mendez/Getty Images 
 From being a Bond girl in "Live and Let Die" to garnering widespread acclaim as strong-willed Dr. Michaela Quinn in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," Jane Seymour experienced a complete career evolution . Starting as early as the 1970s, Seymour racked up various television roles in series like "The Onedin Line" and "Our Mutual Friend." By the 2000s, she left "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" and moved on to other projects. These included playing Kathleen Cleary in the movie "Wedding Crashers" and a semi-regular television character like Genevieve Teague in "Smallville."
 She continued to maintain a decorated resume both in acting and, interestingly enough, fine art. As of 2026, she plays the titular lead in "Harry Wild," a comedic thriller that follows a retired English professor who becomes a makeshift investigator alongside her unlikely partner, Fergus Reid (portrayed by Rohan Nedd). Speaking about her accomplishments to  FOX 11 Los Angeles in July 2026, Seymour noted that her younger self wouldn't have fathomed the career she leads today. "Mind you, by the time I was 25 actually, I was doing quite well, but I never imagined it would be like this," she explained. "Or that I would continue to work all over the world at this time in my life."
 Joe Lando frequently reunites with his former Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman castmates
 CBS/The Roku Channel & therealjoelando/Instagram 
 In "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," Joe Lando portrayed Byron Sully, the rough-around-the-edges mountain man who became Dr. Quinn's main love interest. Lando seamlessly took on the role years after being a regular in "One Life to Live" in the '90s. After "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," he tried his hand at producing, with his first noteworthy project being "Higher Ground." Though Lando moved on from his days on the CBS original, he reunited with his former castmates through various acting projects over the years.
 Aside from "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman: The Movie," one of his first on-screen reunions was in the 2012 film, "Born Wild," which featured William Shockley. In 2014, Lando reunited with most of his CBS castmates in "Dr. Quinn, Morphine Woman with Jane Seymour" for a Funny or Die skit where they parodied "Breaking Bad." Two years later, he co-wrote and co-produced the short "Spotlight." Lastly, in 2026, the Season 5 premiere of "Harry Wild" saw the actor reunite with Jane Seymour. He played pathologist Pierce Kennedy for five episodes.
 In a  TV Insider and Swooon  interview in June 2026, Lando expressed how wonderful it was to share a screen with Seymour again. "The crew and the cast were just so welcoming," he said. "You know, it can be a cold room when you walk on a set sometimes ... but Jane's the leader, and she made sure everyone was in shape."
 Chad Allen left Hollywood and became a clinical psychologist
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Imeh Akpanudosen/Getty Images 
 With acting credits on the  '80s detective show "Simon & Simon,"  "St. Elsewhere," and "Punky Brewster," Chad Allen was already a prominent working actor by the time he portrayed Matthew Cooper in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." After playing the eldest of the three Cooper children, however, Allen's career would take a drastic turn. In 1996, he was outed by The Globe after it published a photograph of him kissing another man. He eventually came out on his own terms in 2001, but his sexuality altered his public perception at the time.
 Though he appeared in "CSI: Miami," "General Hospital: Night Shift," and "Dexter," Allen left acting to focus on a new career path. In 2015, he uploaded a YouTube video saying farewell to his fans and his acting career. "My life has taken me on a very different trajectory, and after 30-plus years as an actor, I made the decision a couple years ago to begin letting that side of my life go," he admitted. "And I've been focusing on my education and working as a clinical psychologist, which is something that I'm super excited about." Allen earned a doctorate in psychology from Antioch University New England. As of 2026, he is a staff psychologist at Williams College.
 Shawn Toovey shifted his focus to his personal life after Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman
 CBS/The Roku Channel & shawnjtoovey/Instagram 
 Shawn Toovey rose to stardom after portraying Brian Cooper, the youngest of three Cooper children, in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." Although he was a working child actor — with credits in "In Broad Daylight" and "Bed of Lies" — Toovey seemingly disappeared from the limelight after the movie sequels "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman: The Movie" and "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman: The Heart Within." Instead, Toovey got involved in various causes during his time away, ranging from diabetes research foundations to youth support services. He also pursued higher education, graduating from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in 2005 with a bachelor's degree in broadcast journalism.
 In recent years, Toovey has embraced the legacy of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." So much so that he flooded his personal social media accounts with behind-the-scenes photos of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." In a May 2026 YouTube interview with a fan page of the show, Toovey admitted that he's thinking about acting again. "I did a few commercials after the show ended, and it was about time to go to college," he recalled. "So, I stepped away to go to college ... But the last couple of years, with sharing the photos on Instagram and Facebook and everything, it's really kind of sparked that desire in me to get back out there and start performing again."
 Erika Flores' seemingly retired from the acting industry
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Fox/Hulu 
 In Season 1 of "Dr Quinn, Medicine Woman," we were introduced to Erika Flores' portrayal of Colleen Cooper, the middle child of the Cooper siblings who were taken in by Dr. Quinn after their biological mother died. She remained a regular cast member until the middle of Season 3, when she left the show without offering an immediate public explanation. Speculation surrounding her sudden departure grew, with many theorizing that it may have been due to behind-the-scenes issues. Tim Johnson, producer of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," later released a statement, stating that Flores left the show to pursue other interests (via The DQ Times ).
 In a 2003 interview with The DQ Times (via VK ), Flores dispelled any rumors, clarifying that she left to focus on her personal life. "I left the show because the priorities I had in my personal life became more important [than] the professional ones," she wrote. "My experience on 'Dr Quinn' was invaluable, but inevitably, as some point, we all have to move on. I made the right choice at the right time in my life, yes, it was a difficult one, but I have never regretted it." Since her departure, Flores has seemingly left the acting industry behind, with her last acting credit in "House" in 2009.
 Jessica Bowman transitioned into a full-fledged entrepreneur
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Brenda Chase/Getty Images 
 After Erika Flores left midway through Season 3 of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," the showrunners needed a replacement for Colleen Cooper. As a result, they turned to Jessica Bowman, whose resume featured shows like the  sitcom "Boy Meets World," "The Road Home," and "Baywatch." From 1998 onward, Bowman continued acting, appearing in "Joy Ride" in 2001 and "Derailed" in 2002. 
 Bowman, however, disappeared from the limelight soon thereafter. In a July 2026 interview with "The Spark,"  she admitted she wanted to explore other careers besides acting. "I left acting because I felt like I'd been doing it for so long that I didn't know anything else," she said. Bowman wanted to attend college and find a career path that aligned with her innate passions. With a psychology degree in hand, she dove into the restaurant business alongside her husband. Still, Bowman suggested that she has other entrepreneurial ventures she wants to pursue. "I'm like, 'But I don't know if restaurants is my passion.' But I do know that I love owning businesses," she explained. "We just bought into a franchise, which would be medical spas because I love skincare and I love beauty. But I never want to shut the door on acting."
 Barbara Babcock left the industry following a crippling diagnosis
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Frank Trapper/Getty Images 
 From "Star Trek" to "Hill Street Blues," Barbara Babcock was already a well-known actor before portraying Colorado Springs journalist Dorothy Jennings in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." With her diverse experience, Babcock continued to act into the 2000s, including a guest appearance alongside the cast of "Frasier,"  a brief gig in "Pasadena," and a supporting role in "Home Alone 4." Unfortunately, Babcock left the acting industry following a serious diagnosis.
 While working on "The Glass Menagerie," Babcock sustained an arm injury. Although she recovered, she noticed a twitch in her finger that wasn't there before. According to her 2018 interview with Carmel Magazine , her eventual trip to a doctor ended in a diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease. "I asked the doctor, 'How long do I have?' ...the cliché of all clichés," she recalled. "His answer was, 'eight to ten years.' That was 14 years ago." Subsequently, Babcock retired from acting and left Los Angeles altogether. "I wanted to leave Los Angeles during the 46 years I spent there," she admitted. "At that time, it was necessary as an actor to be either in New York or LA. I kept thinking of leaving but didn't want to give up the business yet."
 William Shockley tried his hand at filmmaking
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Paul Archuleta/Getty Images 
 William Shockley built a credible acting resume throughout the 1980s before joining "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." Fortunately, his portrayal of the hard-nosed local businessman, Hank Lawson, became his most notable role to date. His stellar performance on the show set him on a path of snagging multiple Western roles like "The Gundown" and "Ambush at Dark Canyon." Shockley also dove into filmmaking, accruing writing credits in multiple projects like "The Legend of 5 Mile Cave" and "Far Haven." In 2017, he made his directorial debut in "Common Threads," which, interestingly enough, opened the door for a future film opportunity in 2025.
 Starring well-known names like Dermot Mulroney and Chris Mulkey, Shockley directed the western "Long Shadows." In a 2025 interview with David A.R. White for  "The White House Pod: Dare to Dream,"  Shockley shared how the film came to be, noting that Granger Hines introduced him to the script for "Long Shadows" (originally written by Shelley Reed) after watching "Common Threads." "Granger, Shelley, and I dove in together and reshaped it and beat it up for a good long while, maybe a year, year and a half ... And then my partners at Tiki Tane read it, and they were like, 'This is great.' And we went to Tucson and scouted, and the rest is history," he recalled.
 Jim Knobeloch led a private life after relocating to Australia
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Jim Knobeloch/Facebook 
 In "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," Jim Knobeloch played Jake Slicker, a small-town barber and medical practitioner. Through his portrayal of Jake Slicker, Knobeloch furthered his acting career. His story wouldn't be complete without ex-wife Beth Sullivan — executive producer of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman — with whom he shares two children. In 2001, the two briefly relocated to Melbourne, Australia, to work on a television series. However, Knobeloch planned to make this his sole residence (via Sullivan v. Knobeloch ). "In approximately February 2002 I decided to make Australia my permanent home," Knobeloch wrote. "I enjoyed living in Australia over California, and it was my belief that plaintiff [Sullivan] and I would live in Victoria, Australia permanently, and raise our children there."
 Knobeloch found consistent work in projects like "Ponderosa" and "King Kong." His personal life changed once he and Sullivan separated in 2007. Their relationship was strained, culminating in Sullivan's alleged departure from Australia back to California with their children. Since then, Knobeloch has led a relatively private life while maintaining his career as an actor. In the 2020s, he portrayed characters in "Smiling Friends," "Foe," and "Ricky Stanicky," which featured John Cena and   "High School Musical" actor Zac Efron .
 Jonelle Allen remained a multi-faceted actor amidst her personal struggles
 CBS/The Roku Channel & jonellerallen/Instagram 
 Jonelle Allen's portrayal of the strong-willed, Colorado Springs café owner Grace in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" was the culmination of consistent work in show business. Having seen success on Broadway, Allen seamlessly transitioned to on-screen roles like "Berrenger's" and "Generations." Once "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" ended, she successfully maintained her decorated acting career. She did so with poise, overcoming alcoholism early in her career, according to her 2023 appearance on the "Truly Kenya Podcast."  "I'm still an alcoholic. That'll never change. However, I have been sober for 35 continuous years," she stated. 
 She also experienced racism in Hollywood, which she's actively pushed back against throughout her career. In 2020, Allen faced her toughest loss as her husband, Leigh Eaton, died in a car accident. During her February 2026 appearance on the "Soapy"  podcast with Rebecca Budig and Greg Rikaart, Allen explained that she also lost her mother months after her husband passed. "What it did is that it makes you know that tomorrow is not promised," she explained. Fortunately, she channeled her grief through her 2021 appearance in "9-1-1." Allen remains active, with acting credits in the podcast series "Forever and a Day" (2021) and "The Keeper" (2025).

 Henry G. Sanders rebuilt his life following the loss of his California home in 2025
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Unique Nicole/Getty Images 
 Alongside Grace in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" was her husband, Robert E., the hardy town blacksmith. Played by Henry G. Sanders, the character is one of the actor's many notable roles throughout the decades. Thanks to memorable guest spots on "Good Times," "St. Elsewhere," and "Night Court," Sanders is a familiar face in the industry. Some of his most acclaimed roles, however, came after "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman." In 2014, he played Cager Lee in "Selma," a biographical film about the life and career of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Sanders remained a familiar face, appearing in Jay-Z and Beyoncé's music video for "Family Feud" and playing Prosper Denton in "Queen Sugar."
 Tragedy struck in 2025, when he lost his Altadena, California, home during the Eaton Fire. This prompted his peers and industry friends to help him and his family get back on their feet. Filmmaker Ava DuVernay uploaded a heartfelt Instagram post, asking her followers to lend a hand through his GoFundMe page. Additionally, Actor Colman Domingo offered Sanders and his family a place to stay in the meantime. In a 2025 interview with Entertainment Tonight , Sanders said he was grateful for the support. "We're blessed," he said. "One, to be alive. Two, to have the love and support of the people that are helping us."
 Frank Collison continued to use his acting work as a funnel for his theater performances
 CBS/The Roku Channel & Randy Shropshire/Getty Images 
 Before becoming the quirky telegraph clerk, Horace Bing, in "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," Frank Collison was a child performer. Thanks to his family's theater roots, he eventually worked on various on-stage productions. Collison later ventured into film and television. From first working with Weird Al Yankovic in "The Compleat Al," Collison became a prominent character actor. Although "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman" was a noteworthy highlight of his career, he continued to find work on various shows like "Good Luck Charlie" and "My Name is Earl" that leaned into his unique personality. 
 It's no issue for Collison, as during his 2021 appearance on "Headshots by Peggy," he embraced his archetype as an actor. "I think that's what you have to do," he said. "You have to just say, 'Okay, that's how I'm seen. That's how people see me.' You know, I've played doctors and lawyers, but I've played a lot of homeless guys. I've played a lot of hillbillies ... You know, everyone is a character." In recent years, Collison and his wife, Laura Gardner, worked as featured artists for the Valdez Theatre Conference, and earned the Jerry Harper Service Award in 2022. Collison also maintained his on-screen career in sitcoms such as "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia" and animated cartoons like "Adventure Time: Fionna & Cake."
